utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning everybody this 1st of May, 2002. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe Witness C has waited long enough, and we should start immediately, if possible, with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I do have one short matter. I don't know if it's possible to cover this morning. Your Honour, I was asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to ask Your Honours for a Rule 73 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have -- we have numerous administrative matters. Please just turn to Witness C. May he be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness C. You can understand us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief may go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Sutherland: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on Friday, you testified about events that happened on the 11th of June. I just wish to go back and ask you a couple of questions to clear the matter up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just go into private session to ask the witness a couple of questions in relation to his relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: His relatives. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objections. Then, please, private session. [Private session].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the incident that happened in the garage on that day, you said this was committed by four Serb police officers who broke into the garage. Were you told the names of these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only two names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't receive a translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only two names.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're not hearing very well. We're having problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you be able to speak up, please. Who were the names of the people you were told committed these crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have a serious interpretation, or connection problems, at least. Could it be resolved immediately? So let's try again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your answer, your last answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You don't have your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your last answer. We didn't receive the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, but we're not hearing anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. The interpreters -- I heard that they weren't hearing the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's have a break of five minutes to try to find out what's the problem. Five minutes. --- Break taken at 9.08 a.m. --- Upon resuming at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now, let's try again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before we had the technical problem, you said that the incident in the garage had been committed by four Serb police officers and that you were given the names of two of them. Can you please tell the Court those two people's names, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They were two out of the four perpetrators and their names are known. They are Jovo Masledjija and Mladjo Jurusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mladjo Jurusic in relation to another incident that happened on the 1st of July. Did you know the other perpetrator, Jovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in the elementary school in Hambarine. He was a teacher there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you the names of these two perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister-in-law told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just explain to the Court, without mentioning the names of your family, what your mother told you when you met up with her later that day about what had happened in the garage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother told me that my brother had been killed and that my wife had been wounded by the same perpetrators and that she remained lying next to the road somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you how these people came into the garage and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people came to the garage with a car and as they were driving up to the garage, from a distance shooting could be heard, shouting and yelling by them. After that they arrived at the garage and they did what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how your brother was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother was killed -- my brother was killed with a bullet shot from a pistol in the forehead. After that first shot, he fell on the concrete and after that, a burst of fire was opened at his chest from an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything else happen to the garage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the murder of my brother, they demanded money, jewellery. They searched the whole garage looking for these things. They yelled at the other people who were there in the garage. They threatened them. They threatened to kill them. In brief, they mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the garage set on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they left, those who survived, the garage was set on fire and my brother was in that garage, dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "After they left, those who survived, the garage was set on fire." Who set the garage on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the four of them, it is not known who exactly, but anyway it was them. Whether all four of them or just one of them, no one knows but anyway, this group of four persons did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your family able to remove your brother's body from the garage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family managed to pull out the body, but not straight away. Only after some time, once they are withdrawn in the direction of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a couple of questions about the other incident that you mentioned on Friday in Carakovo at Aziz Behlic's house. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said on that day, a car came to Carakovo, and then you mentioned that three people had been killed and two were wounded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were about 250 to 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a clear view of these people that arrived in the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they get out of their car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came out of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move back to where we left off on Friday, I want to ask you a couple of questions about events that happened prior to the takeover. Did you see any helicopters landing in your area prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was before the 30th of April. Even in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of 1991? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially after August and September, so the last quarter of that year, from August onwards, September, October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see these helicopters land?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The helicopters landed in the area of Topic Brdo, Gacani, next to Miljakovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away are these villages from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those villages are about 4 or 5 kilometres away, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they on the same level as Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my judgment, there may be a difference in level, but I'm not sure. I think they are somewhat higher, especially Topic Brdo and Miljakovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The villages that you have just mentioned, what ethnicity were the persons living in those villages in 1992? And 1991? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those villages were inhabited by Serbs. Only at Miljakovci, the population was mixed. There were Bosniaks there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see the helicopters land?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day, one could see them land three or four times a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of helicopters were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were military helicopters, dark green in colour, or olive green, with a five-cornered star, which was quite visible as they flew over Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit S14, the map, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you to point out the villages that you mentioned earlier where you saw -- first of all, can you point to Hambarine again on the map. And then point to the villages that you've just mentioned where you saw helicopters landing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where Hambarine is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If you can now point to the villages that -- where you saw helicopters landing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the audiovisual director can zoom out so that the witness can place his finger on Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please place your finger on Hambarine, and then point with the pointer to the other villages where you saw helicopters landing, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to Gacani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gacani is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And excuse my pronunciation; Miljakovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miljakovci is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where else did you observe helicopters landing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Topic Brdo or Topic Hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please point to where that is on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here. This hill is probably above the village of Topic at a higher altitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anywhere else where you saw helicopters landing? You've mentioned Topic Brdo, Miljakovci, Gacani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Pejici. Pejici is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that exhibit could be returned to the registry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what, if anything, did you observe with these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those helicopters were flying at a very low altitude, and they came from the direction of the west, or rather the southwest. And they even flew over a wood called Kurevo that I mentioned earlier. And they flew at a low height, and they headed towards those locations. But I cannot say exactly -- I cannot say exactly where they landed. Anyway, when one watched them and monitored them, one could see them landing in that area that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me just for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know why the helicopters were landing in these villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those helicopters were bringing -- or rather, they were arming the Serb population in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the story that was going around, and it was common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to return to where we left off on Friday. And you had told the Court that you had been interrogated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were detained in the white house for approximately 12 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on that first night in the white house? Were you called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called out the first night and taken to a separate room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this room, once I had been called out by four or five Chetniks, I was beaten up. I was beaten up by them until I lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any other people that were in the room you were detained, were they called out [sic]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, they kept calling people out one by one and beating them up in the same room what I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chetniks started beating me as soon as I entered the room. First, they kicked me, and they were wearing heavy military boots. Then they used rifle butts, police clubs. And when I fell down on the floor, they beat me again. One of them tied a piece of wire around my neck. I lay down on my stomach, and the one who held this wire tight around my neck was actually standing on my hands. His feet were on my hands. Others went on beating me on my back -- actually, all over my body, from head to toe, with baseball bats, police batons, with pieces of electric cable, chains, rifles, everything they had with them. I fainted at one point. I don't know how long I remained unconscious. But when I came to, I was still lying on the same spot. I couldn't believe that I was still alive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to believe that I was still alive, I wanted to do something. I tried to do something. I moved my arm, actually I tried to touch my face with a hand in order to make sure that I was still alive. It seemed impossible. I could hardly believe, myself, that I was still alive. After I done this with my hand, they noticed this and they started cursing me and they set about beating me again with the same objects they had used before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how many men were beating you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, in principle, I want the witness to testify in context and if the witness wants to go on, I don't like to interrupt him. Witness, do you have anything to add? You were just telling your story. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. As I have already indicated, they started beating me again, once they noticed that I had moved. They cursed me, they verbally abused me and they said: "Well, he is still alive." After that, there was a series of blows, once again, all over my body and again, I lost consciousness. After that, I was pulled out to another room, but I don't know how it happened. I don't know how I ended up in this other room. I think it was the other detainees who pulled me out of this room. Two of them were called out and told to throw me out of this first room and put me in the second room so that they could call out another person, another detainee, and do the same to him as what they had done to me. As I told you, we were being called out one by one, to the small room, and beaten up for as long as they pleased, as long they wanted to beat us. After that, two persons took me, as I have said, to another room, where I regained consciousness, but I was still half-conscious. They had actually dragged me from the first room to the second room. I couldn't get up. My condition was severe and I remained for five days like that. I could not get up. I could not even sit, let alone stand up on my feet. I didn't -- couldn't take any food. I couldn't drink anything throughout that time, so difficult was my condition. And I expected to die at any moment, as a result of the beating that I had sustained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during this beating, how many people were beating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four or five of them. You probably want me to say either four or five, but I cannot give you a more accurate number. There were no less than four and not more than five. The room was half dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I was not able to recognise anyone for that reason. And also I couldn't look them in their face. I could only see their boots and once I fell down, I remained lying on my stomach. So I couldn't make out their faces. I couldn't see who they were. And as I said, it was almost dark in the room. It was nighttime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When other people from your room returned from being called out, what was their condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No better than mine. Their condition was also severe. They had been badly beaten up. They were crying, asking for water. They were in a desperate condition, covered with blood, they could not stand up on their feet. They were in the same shape as I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following morning, what was their condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following morning, the condition -- their condition was not getting any better. They were in the same condition as they had been the day before, after they had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone die as a result of these beatings the previous night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, I don't know how many of us exactly were beaten, but the next morning, out of all of us who had been called out, there were six or seven detainees who died as a result of the beatings. And once it became light, we recognised that they were dead. They were lying on the floor in this room and they were dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the names of these people that died as a result of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the names, I don't know all of them. I know

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, Your Honour. And if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could have redacted from the videotape and the transcript, the names of his relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after your time in the white house, where were you moved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the white house, I was transferred to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being moved to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when around the date that you were moved to the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that it was before the 20th of July. Maybe on the 19th or maybe even on the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there for about 8 or 10 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the hangar building, where were you then moved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the hangar building I was moved to a room which was referred to as Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: These rooms were located inside the administration building of the mine company, the mining company, above the restaurant which had been used prior to the war, which had been used as a canteen for the employees of the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the entrance to Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entrance to Mujo's room was on the other side from the entrance to the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a building called "the red house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see people being taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those people return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw anyone return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever see bodies being loaded on to TAM trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see bodies being loaded, but I have other knowledge concerning this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from other detainees of bodies being loaded on to TAM trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard from other detainees such stories. These stories circulated all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the red house, you said that you never saw these people return. Did you see them again in the camp, or ever again, or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the conditions in Omarska camp. Can you please describe for the Court what the food was like, what your living conditions were like, the hygiene in the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The living conditions in the Omarska camp were terrible, were totally inappropriate and were so difficult that we didn't have -- there was no hygiene at all. People were dying as a result of such bad conditions, and also as a result of beatings. There were people who had been wounded, but there were no conditions for their treatment at all. So nothing was ever done about that. Those who were lucky and fortunate survived, but they can only thank God for their survival. As far as the food is concerned, we had only one meal a day, which was always the same. It was some kind of soup or a stew; but frankly speaking, it didn't resemble soup at all. It was boiling hot, and we had only two minutes to get there from the rooms where we were to the restaurant and to eat our meal, finish eating, and leave the restaurant. We only had two minutes to do all this. We entered the restaurant in groups of 30 to 40 people. And there were armed Chetniks inside the restaurant who kept walking around the tables and beating us as we were eating this pitiful meal. Many of us couldn't even finish the meal, couldn't eat it up. They would leave the restaurant without having eaten anything. Of course, when something is boiling hot, you need more time. But we simply could not wait. We were hungry. We dreamt about food. We fantasised about eating. And sometimes, there were even days when one was not able to get to the restaurant, and many people didn't eat that one meal that they had, either because the food was lacking or because it was impossible for us to go because sometimes the detainees couldn't walk, some of them. And even that one, as I said, pitiful meal a day was denied to them. And it was so poor in quality that you really couldn't consider it food for humans. As I said, I spent five days in the white house without any food. I couldn't get up, so I didn't eat this little food that we had in the Omarska camp during those five days. When you're starving, you're happy to have this one poor meal if possible. But very often, there were days when we didn't even get that. There were people who were afraid to go to the restaurant, though they were very hungry and had not eaten for days. But they simply didn't dare go there because they were afraid that they would be beaten up or killed at any moment, at any spot. It could happen to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned a moment ago that you had some knowledge in relation to bodies being loaded on to TAM trucks. What were you told? And by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that people who had been killed were loaded on to those trucks and that those trucks were eventually driven to the pits. One could notice on the truck that it was dirty and there were bloodstains on it, bloodstains left by the bodies of the killed detainees. And the detainees who were on the spot told us that these people, these bodies, had been taken away and that they were not returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were detained in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you were transferred from Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could the interpreters speak up a little. I can hardly hear him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Do you recall the date when you were transferred from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date was it, and where were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 6th of August, 1992. On that day, I was transferred to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken there in a bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this -- who owned this bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several buses, different buses, belonging to different owners. But the most famous company was the Autotransport Prijedor Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned there were a number of buses. How many people were on each of the buses, if you can approximate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can approximate -- I don't know the exact number, but I think that there were -- that each bus carried many more people than it would normally. So at any rate, there were more than 50 people -- actually, between 50 and a hundred people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you escorted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each bus had escorts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were the same Chetniks from the Omarska camp, the same people who had abused us and beaten us. They were the ones who escorted us to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were the guards from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the conditions in the bus when you travelled to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions in the bus were unbearable. There were too many of us on each bus. People sat between two rows of seats. In the middle of the bus, there were people under the seats. There were so many people. It was so crowded, and it was very hot. The heat was so unbearable that people fainted. They were exhausted. It was stuffy and stifling, and I -- we even thought that the driver turned on the heating in the bus, but we were not allowed to open the windows. We had to keep our heads bent down and our hands behind our heads. And it was in this condition that we were transported to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone mistreated on the buses on the way to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were mistreated on the buses by those same guards who escorted the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that when you arrived in Manjaca, you had to stay on the bus all night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the following day, you were moved into a stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, later in the afternoon, we were transferred -- or rather, we entered the Manjaca camp, that is, the stables in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered Manjaca, did you see any detainees that were from Prijedor or the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Prijedor municipality, I didn't see anyone when we entered the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses were there that you can recall that left Omarska camp and went to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were more or less 20 buses. Around 20 buses, plus or minus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were detained in Manjaca from the 6th of August until the 18th of December. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were being detained in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you required to sign anything prior to leaving Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you required to sign, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to sign a document on the day I left the Manjaca camp. And that means only a couple of minutes before leaving, so maybe five minutes before I signed this piece of paper. I can't remember exactly to be able to quote what was on that paper. The only thing I can say, if I'm allowed to, is what I assume it could have been. So it is just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you assume it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the paper said that I and that all the others, therefore, would not return to the territory of the so-called Serbian region or Serbian Krajina, something to that effect. And if we should happen to return and if I should be arrested again, then I would not go to the camp, but that I would be sentenced to death in advance. So, I would not be deported to the camp, but would be killed. Allow me to add such a statement to the effect that if any of the detainees were to be arrested again, they would be killed, and such a statement was made by the commander of the Manjaca camp. This was what he said orally, on that day when we were leaving Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had to sign this form. Did all the other detainees who left on that day also have to sign the form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all had to sign the same form that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Manjaca, I was taken in the direction of Banja Luka and via Banja Luka to Bosanska Gradiska. From Bosanska Gradiska, we crossed the bridge over the Saleh river to Croatia. In Croatia, we all got in to other buses and were transferred to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Karlovac, were you told about your other brothers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was told about my other brothers, what had happened to them. I was told that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had they been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed in Biscani or, to be more precise, a part of Biscani called Mrkalji, or still better known as Mrkalji Mlin or mill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister-in-law told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what you were told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in Biscani, my two late brothers, together with their wives. One brother had two children, the other brother didn't have any children. They were in the basement, in the owner's house on the 20th of July when there was cleansing of Rakovcani, Rizvanovici and Biscani, which is known as the great massacre in these three locations. Chetniks broke in to the basement and, among the crowd in the basement, there were women, children and elderly people. They took out the two of them outside and led them to another house which was close by. I do not wish to mention the name of the owner of that house unless you insist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please don't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to another yard that was very close by, some 15 metres away and that is where they were killed, together with some other men -- and I don't know who they were, the others -- without any cause -- I beg your pardon -- without any questions asked. They were simply killed with automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your sister-in-law tell you how your brothers were dressed they day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in civilian clothes. What is more, my brother had a track suit on him, as did my other brother. My sister-in-law -- I do apologise -- my sister-in-law has the top of that track suit. She had it with her -- she had this with her at that time. I don't know whether she still has it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your brothers were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that someone collected these bodies on a truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that after a few days the bodies were collected. All those bodies were left lying there, or actually the bodies in all three places, Rakovcani, Rizvanovici and Biscani, lay there for several days and were, after that, collected and driven away in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the persons from Biscani village went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. All the persons who were there, women and children and the elderly, if you think they were few, these elderly men, all of them went to Tukovi near the stadium and stayed there until they were deported to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my final question for you is this: Were you or any members of your family a member of any armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe it is appropriate to have a break now. Let's resume five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Witness C may be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. C.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic and, together with Mr. John Ostojic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Stakic. We shall now begin with our cross-examination, which won't be as lengthy and detailed as the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, but I would like to appeal to you to assist us in clarifying a few facts. Can we begin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can. But I would like to ask you, if you could, and if Their Honours allow, to speak in English, because this is a bit confusing for me. The reason being that I can immediately answer your questions, forgetting the need for translation into English, or maybe French.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, I would like to continue in B/C/S, and we would hope that we will all be a bit more cautious and try to pause in between questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence counsel, please understand, we may continue in B/C/S, but please take on your headphones that in case there is overlapping, you can immediately hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us begin. Do you know that in the former Yugoslavia, it was normal for the perpetrator of a murder to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about the incident at Hambarine, and please have in mind Mr. Ferid Sikiric who was wounded on that occasion. Do you know that Mr. Sikiric was wounded in the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of that incident, were armed Muslims withdrawing from a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Armed Bosniaks - I wish to correct you, not Muslims - remained at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that armed Bosniaks were at the checkpoint throughout the duration of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While the incident was occurring, it was only normal that they should be at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that people who were present during the incident are claiming that Mr. Sikiric was wounded in the back by one of the armed Bosniaks present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sikiric was wounded by one of the Chetniks who were in that car that was passing by the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that, and it's only logical. As the car passed by the checkpoint, they opened fire from the car at a group of Bosniaks who were at the checkpoint. And on that occasion, Ferid Sikiric was wounded in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C, we have just established that armed Bosniaks were at the checkpoint or the time and that they were not withdrawing. How can you explain then, that someone who is facing the enemy because obviously according to you there was an armed incident occurring, could be hit in the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't understand your question. Could you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will do my best. We have established that Muslims or rather Bosniaks who were armed and who were at the checkpoint were there all the time and that they were not withdrawing. How can you explain that someone could be wounded in the back by the enemy that is in front of the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the Bosniaks were not withdrawing, they were at the checkpoint. And as the car arrived from the direction of Ljubija in the direction of Prijedor , that means on the return trip, fire was opened from the car in front of the checkpoint and Ferid Sikiric was at the checkpoint facing Tukovi, that is Prijedor, in the direction of Prijedor, and in the shooting, he was wounded in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you about this, the way he was facing, as you just explained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that after a certain period of time when I arrived home after that incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us please how the other persons at the checkpoint Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were facing, in which direction were the other people facing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you. Because I was not told about that. Only Ferid was wounded and we talked about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you mentioned Aziz Aliskovic, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which way he was facing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you said: "I came to the conclusion that no one had any trust any more in the JNA." Who, in your opinion, did not trust the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, I, personally, had no trust in them, and the other Bosniaks in Bosnia, all Croats in Bosnia, and then the Croats in Croatia and the Slovenes in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serbs have faith in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can it be concluded then that your conclusion that no one had faith in the JNA is not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said who did have faith in them and who did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the Serbs for you no one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, it was known who the Serbs were, who the Bosniaks were and who the Croats were. You know that very well. Because we lived together in Bosnia, all of us, together, and there were no big problems until everything started in 1990, when political parties started to be formed, that is, the multiparty system was introduced. It was then that everything was turned upside down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period of time you are referring to, was the JNA the legal military force in Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was until 1991, when it attacked Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you also said that: "In September I received callup papers, along with another 350 men, and we ignored it." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these 350 other Muslims who received callup papers together with you from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction, Bosniaks. They were from the area of Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that these 350 other men, the Bosniaks, ignored the callup for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because no one responded and this was what I knew, that no one went to the front lines in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you change your opinion if I were to tell you that a large number of Muslims and Croats did respond to the call for mobilisation in September 1991 and there are official documents about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they did respond, then they were few in number. I don't know with precision how many, and they were, in my opinion, my personal opinion, they were forced to do that. Even the military police would come looking for those people in their homes and would deport them to barracks and from there to the battlefront in Croatia. That was done with the help of the military police, regardless of the will of those people who did not want to go. They may be the people that you said had responded to the callup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that an agreement had been reached among the parties in cooperation with the JNA that whoever was -- wanted to go to the front could go, and those who didn't want to go, needed to say so clearly and return their weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such agreement that you have mentioned as having been reached among the political parties, I assume you mean, and the former JNA. I'm not aware of that. Maybe you know something more about that. Maybe you could clarify it; maybe I'd like to hear more about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Muslims and Croats that were sent to the front were given weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please, for the third time, I'm asking you to use the term "Bosniaks". If you use the word -- if you're talking about nationality, use the word "Bosniaks." If you're talking about religion and religious affiliation, then you can call them Muslims, Catholics, and Orthodox. But regarding ethnicity, you may use the terms "Bosniaks," "Serbs," and "Croats." Your Honours, I apologise for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the year 1992 and 1991. Were there Bosniaks in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the population census sometime in March 1991, it was stated that there were Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I apologise. Let me add: Bosniaks, if we can go back in history, are mentioned centuries ago, even during the Turks, which ruled Bosnia for 500 years, and also during the Austro-Hungarian empire. This can be easily be checked in the archives that exist in Turkey and in Vienna, the capital of Austria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on from these history lessons to the question that I put to you. The Croats and Bosniaks who were sent to the front, were they issued weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was not with them. I was not in touch with them. So I can't say, and I can't confirm that they were issued weapons. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the response to mobilisation in other Bosniak and Croat settlements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in Prijedor municipality or in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to move to your testimony about Celpac. You remained working at Celpac up until the outbreak of the conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, until the incident which took place in Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you were requested to remain at work, although, as you said, there was not much work to do. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any electricity in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town of Prijedor, yes, there was electricity there until the 22nd of May. I don't know about the period of time which followed later. I know that there were shortages from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This lack of work and power shortages, were these the consequences of the general conditions in the state at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. Maybe the accused knows more about it than I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the situation was in other Prijedor-based companies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 22nd of May, 1992, on the bus that took you home from work, were there both Serbs and Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was everyone ordered to get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Tukovi, everyone left the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the mixed groups of the army and the police which were manning the checkpoints, were they also ethnically mixed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me which checkpoint you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's say the checkpoint at which you were stopped in Tukovi on the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the checkpoint in Tukovi was ethnically mixed. I did not have an opportunity to ask them about their ethnic background. It would have been absurd. But at any rate, it was known that this particular checkpoint was manned by only one ethnic group, and you know which one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the existence of any other checkpoint manned by a mixed group of military and the police? Do you know that any such checkpoint was also ethnically mixed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you have any such knowledge, please feel free to put it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not allowed to testify here, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the soldiers who were manning the Tukovi checkpoint had red and white armbands. Did any of the civilians on the bus wear any of such armbands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No civilian had such a band.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that the guards at the checkpoint were clean shaven -- they didn't have any moustache or beard -- but that you knew them to be Chetniks. Can you describe for us a Chetnik? What does he look like and why did you call these guards "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Chetniks. It's a fact, regardless of whether they had a beard or not, or a moustache. It was by their uniform that one could judge that, regardless of whether the uniform was a police uniform or an army uniform. For me, they were Chetniks. And as I said, it was a fact. Do you want to know why I call them Chetniks, why I refer to them as Chetniks? It is a well-known word. It is well known to everyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina, through Croatia, and further on -- in Croatia and further on. The term has been used ever since the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe we have to stop. The transcript doesn't follow. Let's try again. You can see on the video where the transcript stopped and you added two sentences. The last sentence was "The term has been used ever since the Second World War." Could you proceed there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C, as you can see, we have had some technical problems and we will have to repeat the last question and the last answer. Was every Serb police officer or a Serb soldier -- is every Serb police officer or a Serb soldier a Chetnik for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the word "Chetnik", does it have negative connotations for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you hate Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason to like them after everything that has happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, after what has happened to me personally and to my family. And in general, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, after what has been done by Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you hate them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Why would I like them? I have no reason to like them. And, well, if you want a specific answer, yes, I hate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 22nd of May when you were stopped at the Tukovi checkpoint. The Serb soldiers who were at the checkpoint, did they see you were from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't know that I was from Hambarine. They didn't ask me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they see you leave in the direction of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can we conclude that you did leave towards Ljubija and Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards Ljubija, but not the usual way, not along the road which is normally used by the local bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers were police officers or civilians who were inside the car which was shot at, at the Hambarine checkpoint, were they in a bulletproof armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I heard from the members of my family after I had returned home, it was a civilian vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you think that the story that you heard from others involving four individuals driving in a civilian car who, according to the story, opened fire to a checkpoint which was manned by armed individuals --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- don't you think that this storey is not credible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I believe that? Why would I think it is not credible? Why would anyone make it up? And besides, I trust the members of my family who told me about that, about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were members of your family present when this incident happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you heard that the car had stopped after 30 metres. Doesn't that indicate that the car was shot at, even before it reached the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The fire was opened from the car before the checkpoint and as the car was passing, Ferid Sikiric was wounded in this shooting and the car continued towards Prijedor. At that moment, fire was returned from the checkpoint towards the car which was -- which stopped at that moment some 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the car was shot at once it had passed the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The car was shot at as it was passing by the checkpoint, as it was moving in the direction of Prijedor and, as I had already indicated, it was the fire which came as a response to the fire which had been opened from the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like you to go back to the time prior to the attack on Hambarine, if you can, please. In your statement, you declared that at least 1.000 shells fell on Hambarine and that you heard later that fire had been opened from the Bosniak checkpoint. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of shells landed on the village of Hambarine. It was difficult to count them. We counted up until hundred and then we stopped. It was no longer possible to count the shells because at the same time -- they were hitting the area at the same time and you could no longer distinguish between these shells. So several shells were falling at the same time and I think, I am sure, about this figure, as regards the number of shells that hit Hambarine. As for the shooting at the checkpoint, it came at the moment when Chetnik forces moved towards Hambarine in a pack and an APC together with infantry forces. It was at that moment that the Bosniak guards, who were there at the checkpoint, in the field in Hambarine, put up a defence. They tried to defend themselves from a Chetnik attack which was coming from the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean that shooting could be heard after the shelling had stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the shelling, we could hear fire being opened from infantry weapons and also from armed personnel carriers, a fire which is somewhat different from the one opened from infantry weapons, which was a sign that Chetnik forces were moving towards Hambarine. Our forces, while the shelling still went on, did not open fire. They had no reason to open fire, because the shelling was still going on from a great distance. So it was not necessary to return fire because of the kind of weapons that they had. They only had a handful of rifles. It was only after the Chetnik forces had started moving towards the village with the infantry forces and assisted by two or three tanks - I don't know exactly how many; it's not important - and some APCs, that is, armoured carriers, that our guards, who were down there, tried to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you also declared that in this fighting which took place at the checkpoint, two police officers were killed, two Bosniak police officers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that there were no checkpoints in Hambarine before the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because I went to Prijedor every day. I went to work every day. And on the way to Prijedor and on the way back, I would pass by the spot at the road where the checkpoint was. When I went to work, this checkpoint was not there before the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about two checkpoints. Where was the other one located and when was it set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this other checkpoint, I don't think I should refer to it as a "checkpoint". Personally, I don't think it was a checkpoint, although you call it that way. However, it was merely a spot where guards were sometimes on duty in order to control the area in case of an incursion of Chetniks from the other side of the village of Hambarine. The people who stood guard on this location were not armed. They were all civilians. They wore civilian uniforms, that is, civilian clothes, and stood there unarmed in case Chetniks should try to attack the village from the direction of Ljeskare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in the arming of people in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who are the people who had weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those people who were at the checkpoint that has already been mentioned had weapons in Hambarine. The checkpoint mentioned in the incident, that is, Hambarine, in the field, they had weapons. The weapons they had was the property of the former Territorial Defence, the Territorial Defence of Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that people from Hambarine participated in the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know who took part in that attack that you mention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what is your understanding of the situation if in Hambarine, the village of Hambarine, there were only ten or so rifles, how was it possible that the ultimatum be rejected issued by the army to hand over the killers and the weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean as "the killers"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army demanded that the killers of the people in the car be surrendered, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You call them "killers," but in fact, for me, they are not killers. They did so in self-defence. For me, the killers are those who were in the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please try and answer my question. How would you explain the rejection of the ultimatum issued by the army to hand over those men and the weapons, the people who opened fire at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an opinion of my own in that regard. I was not someone who decided about that, nor was I consulted. And I do not wish to say anything about that, because I was not competent in regard to that surrender of weapons or the ultimatum received from the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you withdrew to the woods between Carakovo and Hambarine. Who was in control of this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: This area was under the control of the Chetniks; however, they were not always there, but occasionally they would open fire and shell and infiltrate themselves. Or to be more precise, in that area, in the woods between Carakovo and Hambarine, there was no checkpoint held by the Chetnik forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a dugout in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were just meadows, a stream, and woods in that area. There were no dugouts. What is more, there were many people from Hambarine with their livestock who could no longer keep them at home during the attack on Hambarine. Everything fled, and they were there, too, together with their livestock and whatever they were able to carry. And that was some food, if they had any, they took with them, and that is how it was while they stayed in those woods between Carakovo and Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said that the Muslims self-organised themselves to form armed forces? You, yourself, used the term "Muslim," so I'm just citing what you said. I hope you won't take it against me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that I said "Bosniaks." But it may be a technical error in the translation, if you're referring to my statement, my written statement, if you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 4, fifth paragraph, second line of your statement. However, I can paraphrase if you don't like this, but what did you mean when you said that: "The Bosniaks self-organised themselves into armed forces"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you be more precise, please? Will you tell me when and where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Counsel, may I ask you once, again as I did in the beginning with the first witness, please quote the entire sentence and indicate for the record the exact paragraph and the page you are quoting. It facilitates our lives. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Bear with me, Your Honours. Give me a few seconds. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honours, I was following the B/C/S version, and it's page 4, paragraph 5, second line. So I'll try to find it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to assist counsel, it's page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, also the fifth paragraph. And it starts in the first row.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be also of assistance for the witness if you could quote to the record the sentence you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "At my village, there were two checkpoints manned by Muslims. The Muslim people had self-organised themselves into Defence Forces." Page 4, fifth paragraph, first line, and onwards. Can you tell us what you meant under "armed forces"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says "defence forces" over there, as far as my recollection serves me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, please, what you mean by "defence forces"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that they organised themselves and set up or organised that checkpoint that we have already talked about at Hambarine in the field, and a second checkpoint, that you call a checkpoint even though it wasn't a checkpoint, for me a checkpoint has to have weapons, this other checkpoint, I have to use that term because you are using it, so that you know what I am talking about. That one was without weapons. And it is my belief that this was organisation of self-defence. That was this act of self-defence, that is, the formation of that checkpoint in Hambarine and this second so-called checkpoint at the other side of Hambarine, between Hambarine and Ljeskare. I think I already mentioned that a moment ago in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us focus for a moment on this checkpoint. Official police cars going from Prijedor to Ljubija, did they have to pass by this checkpoint on the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army and the police, after the takeover of power on the 30th of April, did they enter Hambarine before the attack on the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say because I wasn't at the checkpoint. I went to work. I was at work all day from 6.00 a.m. to 6.00 p.m. I had my working hours. So I can't answer that question of yours. Briefly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your relatives mention the army or the police entering the village or did they not mention anything along those lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean before this incident at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, before the incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C, are you aware that in the woods of Kurevo, there were armed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any armed Bosniaks there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in these woods, there were for a time, Mirza Mujadzic, Hasan Talundzic and others from the Prijedor police, Prijedor Stup?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they were in the woods of Kurevo. In my testimony, I already said who was in the Kurevo woods and I don't think it is necessary for me to repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in August 1991 the war had already started in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that military helicopters would land three or four times a day in the area close to Hambarine, very close to Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this landing occurred during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated a period roughly of some 90 days; you said August, September, October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that there were three or four landings a day and over a periods of 90 days that would mean between 270 and 360 landings, would that be a correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Counsel, may I interrupt you. The witness said twice, five to six times every day and you quoted this and why do you say now, three or four landings a day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that I heard three to four times a day. Sorry. But we can accept five to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So, please once again I really ask you, take the advantage. You have the document before you and quote the entire sentence and of the origin. This would be in this case, page four, paragraph two, the fifth line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was quoting from today's transcript, Your Honour, so that is why. Maybe there is some discrepancy. But I accept and I don't think that it is crucial. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these helicopters were flying at a very low altitude when they were observed and followed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you following and monitoring the landing of the helicopters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who organised this observation and monitoring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think that is an inappropriate question. No organisation is required for such a thing. This monitoring was in front of my house, in the yard. Actually, we were in the house. We were at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these helicopters arm the Serbs ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw the helicopters that were going in that direction and landing there and -- however, I cannot from Hambarine, from my house in Hambarine to be even more precise, see them taking out or unloading the weapons from the helicopters, unloading it and what after that they did with those weapons, whom they gave them to and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be possible that these helicopter landings were intended for the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that, whether they were linked to the war in Croatia or not. The people in charge of that operation would know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement on page four of the English version, fifth paragraph, fourth line, you said and I quote, "At the checkpoints there were approximately 10 people and they were led by the Crisis Staff headquarters." Could you tell us a little more about this Crisis Staff

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the Crisis Staff of Hambarine was set up after the 30th of April, that is, after the military coup, the military putsch in Prijedor municipality carried out by the Serbian police and the military in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a military putsch, but could you please answer my question and tell me about the Crisis Staff in Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said when the Crisis Staff was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us who the members were and what their roles were, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you as much as I know. All the members of the Crisis Staff were not known to me. I just knew of two members. As regards their positions, I can't tell you that either, what functions each of them had. In my view, there were not more than four or five members of the Crisis Staff. That is my opinion, my arbitrary opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of those two people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I can. Their names were Ferid Sikiric, Agnan Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A meeting was held in Hambarine, do you know that a meeting of the SDA Crisis Staff was in Hambarine of Prijedor municipality to take over power in Prijedor by force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall now very briefly ask you a few questions about Omarska. Was there ever any epidemics in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of epidemics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medically, I can't tell you its name. But I do know, and I can use an ordinary word which is used by the people, and that is many, many detainees had an epidemics, an attack of diarrhea. Also, all the detainees had lice in their hair, the hair of their heads. We were all without exception infected in this way. There were even symptoms of hepatitis in the Omarska camp. I apologise for using such words. I hope you will be able to understand what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
