utterances.text: The prisoners in Omarska, before their meal, did they wash their hands in a disinfectant solution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no such solutions in Omarska at all, no such liquids.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, we are now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. It's appropriate to have the break now. And before we start with the break, only one question to the OTP. What about their intentions, re-examination, and Dr. Donia this afternoon? Or how do you want to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I have no re-examination for the witness. And it's my understanding that Mr. Cayley is going to deal with Dr. Donia this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What's the time you expect to use for your final cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter that I wanted to raise that's short. And I was hoping I could raise it because if Mr. Cayley is here this afternoon with Ms. Sutherland, there really won't be room at the table for me. And that is in regards to the motions -- the Court's oral order, I believe last Thursday, for the identification parade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I said already we have to take care of the time limits of the interests of the witness, and then the interest of Dr. Donia, and then finally it's our interests to discuss the administrative matters. Please understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understand. Just so the Court knows, there is a time limit on this of today. So I do need a decision on this today because of the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we stay adjourned and resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We resume immediately, and may the Defence continue with the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness C, when you spoke about the release from Manjaca, you told us about what you assumed was written on the release papers, but you don't actually remember the exact words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I don't remember the text. If necessary, I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this, I should like to ask you whether you know whether, before your release from Manjaca, it had already been agreed with the international Red Cross that you would be transferred to a third country. Are you aware of any such agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this agreement; however, we were not sure that this would happen. We heard about this agreement immediately before our release from the Manjaca camp. During our last days at Manjaca, we learned from the Red Cross that there were such ideas, but we didn't really believe that we would be released. We didn't harbour much hope to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer. Was the commander of the Manjaca camp familiar with your release and departure to a third country? Was he aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Aziz Aliskovic was a member of the Crisis Staff in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Aziz Aliskovic was a member of the Hambarine Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long was the operation which started on the 22nd of May -- actually, the 22nd of May was the date of the checkpoint incident. But do you know when the attack on Hambarine started and how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right about the incident. It took place on the 22nd of May. As for the attack and the shelling of Hambarine, it started around 12.00 approximately. And it lasted until half past 6.00 approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean on the same day, on the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. On the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the operation completed at 7.00 that evening? When did it finish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Hambarine finished at about half past 6.00 or 7.00. I cannot tell you the exact hour and the minute. But it must have been thereabouts, between half past 6.00 and 7.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the civilians had left Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the civilians go back to Hambarine; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of the civilians returned to Hambarine. There were individual returns secretly. People would go back to their homes to get some food, and then they would leave again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw that two police officers were killed on that day. What about other people who had weapons? Where were they? You said that there were at least ten rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were up to ten rifles, not at least ten rifles. There were not more than ten rifles. Will you please take note of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. But do you know where other armed people eventually ended up? What happened with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other people who had weapons withdrew towards the Kurevo woods with the rest of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness C.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my cross-examination of you. Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, the question, any re-examination by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness C, I'm sorry to say that the Judges have some additional questions. We really need to have the entire picture of Prijedor, what happened in the camps; and therefore, I have already to apologise now beforehand that there will be the one or other question you will regard as repetitive. But for us, some clarification seems to be necessary. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please tell us once again since when and until when did you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be happy to answer your question and tell you when I lived in Prijedor. I was -- I lived in Prijedor ever since my birth until 1977. From 1977 up until 1981, I was absent from Prijedor. And then again, from 1981 until 1992, when the war started in Bosnia, I was in Prijedor. That is, I lived in my native town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this very precise answer. Could you please tell me, has there been any JNA barracks in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a JNA barracks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One, two, three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two barracks in Prijedor. One of them was quite large, and the other one was rather small and was located in another area, away from this big one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many people would you say were -- could be regarded as JNA personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I remember from the time before the war, during military exercises and while in barracks, I remember that there were two battalions approximately in the barracks, but that is just my estimate, including the reserve force, which was there, or which members of which came to the barracks from time to time to be issued with weapons for the purposes of military exercises. Military exercises. The weapons, we would return them upon the completion of the military exercise in the same barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness C, do you remember the elections held in November 1990 in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there any substantive change in the society you would remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a substantive change which occurred after the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please explain a little bit, in context.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these multiparty elections, which were the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they took place on the 18th of November, 1990, it was the SDA that got the majority of votes. And after the election, changes occurred within the structure of the municipal government. There were some changes made in various companies in Prijedor, and different people took up leading and managing positions, people who were representatives of these parties, that is, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, in part. And other opposition parties. The SDS won the majority of votes during the election; and after the election, they were the leading party. The elections were legal, carried out in accordance with relevant laws. The SDS got some positions within the structure of the local municipal government, and also some leading positions in various companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After these elections, have there been any difficulties, especially in the JNA, between Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems. They couldn't come to an agreement as regards the distribution of leading positions and leading offices within the municipal government and the executive authority. So as I said, they couldn't agree on these issues, and they tried to negotiate. However, to no avail, because the SDS wanted many of these functions, these positions, although they did not have the majority of the votes as a result of the elections. Therefore, there were lots of disagreements, lots of differences, between these -- amongst these parties as the SDS, SDA and HDZ. As the SDS was against the majority of -- all of the decisions which were reached by the SDA and HDZ. And the SDS, as a result of that, enjoyed the support of the former JNA which had sided with them and gave them their support in respect of everything. So they had this military support, the support which they used and abused, to the detriment of other peoples, other communities, in the municipality, especially against Muslims, Bosniaks, and also against Croats, including a number of minority groups that lived in the area of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there anything one could call a series of dismissing people from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the takeover by the SDS, after this military coup which was carried out with the assistance of the former JNA, the military, and the civilian police force, many people were dismissed from their positions, from their jobs. I can illustrate this with an example which relates to a more important office. I don't know whether Your Honours want me to tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mayor of the municipality of Prijedor, Mr. Muhamed Cehajic, was legally elected during these multiparty elections which took place on the date that I indicated. However, after this military coup, after the takeover of power which happened overnight and with force, Muhamed Cehajic was ousted from this office, as was the case with a number of officials who worked at the MUP in the Prijedor municipality. When I say "MUP," I refer to the Ministry of the Interior, the department of MUP in the municipality of Prijedor. Police officers were dismissed, but not only police officers; this was the case with administrative staff as well and other personnel such as inspectors and other officials. Many such changes occurred in various companies. The mayor, Mr. Muhamed Cehajic, was subsequently taken to the Omarska camp where he was killed. His successor was a man from the SDS. I can tell you his name, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic, the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did you hear the name Dr. Stakic the first time in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard about him was when the SDS was established in the Prijedor municipality. And also, after the first multiparty election, although at the time, he did not occupy this particular position, the one he took over in 1992. After Mr. Muhamed Cehajic was ousted from office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see him in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not personally know him, and I wish to say that I am pleased with the fact that I didn't know him personally. Likewise, I wish to say that I consider myself fortunate because I did not know these people before the war, the people who were in Keraterm, Omarska, and Manjaca. I am referring specifically to the guards in these camps. I hope, Your Honours, that you can understand why. Once again, let me stress that I am actually pleased with the fact that I did not know them, because I think that it saved my life. I think this is one of the reasons why I am now sitting here in this courtroom before this Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness C, what do you understand when you hear the notion "Chetnik songs"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reminds me of all the terrible things that I experienced during the war in 1992. It also reminds me of the Second World War and the history books while I was still a student, although I think I can say that the history we were taught was falsified. It was written in such a way to suit those who had committed crimes, which means that it was written in such a way that it suited to those who did -- who committed crimes in the Second World War. Whatever I hear the word "Chetnik" and when I have to use it, and I have to say this here, I mean, I have to use this term here, but it is actually hard for me to use this word, and also it is hard for me to hear it being said, especially when I remember my stay in the camp, my detention in the camp. And when I remember their songs which they used to sing while playing with our bodies -- while dancing on our bodies, while hitting us detainees, because very often, they forced us detainees to sing Chetnik songs, threatening that they would kill us if we did not obey. So we had to sing, all of us together, these Chetnik songs. And they, those very same Chetniks, laughed at our singing, although we were made to sing their songs, Chetnik songs. Later on, they made fun of us. They mistreated us, and they shouted at us, saying that we knew how to sing their songs, that we were able to sing their songs, although we didn't know them. But we had to learn them; we had to learn their songs whether we liked it or not and to sing them. Psychologically, this was very difficult, almost impossible, because apart from all other mistreatments, we were also abused psychologically. I think we all suffer consequences from our detention in the camp, not only physically but also psychologically, consequences which are here to stay for as long as we live. I don't think it is necessary for me to go into details describing my own personal consequences in terms of health and also psychological consequences. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Though evidently it's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Though evidently it's the hated issue, these Chetnik songs, do you remember the one or the other text or title of these songs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to remember, because this reminds me of the Omarska camp, and it's very hard for me. Yet, I can just tell you a few words, to the best of my recollection, because I endeavoured to delete the songs that we had to sing from my memory. I'm trying to be rid of it, and I'm doing my best to forget it for my own reasons and for reasons of health. But let me tell you a sentence. I may be wrong in quoting it. I may be wrong. Maybe I would need more time at home to sit down and to remind myself of those verses and to note them down. But I'm going to say, as I promised, what I remember, and I quote: "From Serbia to Ravna Gore there are guards of General Draza" and so on and so forth. There's a lot more to come and follow. I've already given you the reasons for my inability to tell you everything, but -- because after all, this was ten years ago. One can't remember everything in view of the torture experienced in those camps. Just now, just now I can't remember any other songs. Maybe later on. But it's not that important. When I go outside, when I leave this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand that it's difficult to remember, not only because it's ten years ago, but can you probably remember the one or other concrete situation when you were forced to sing Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were forced. I was among the other detainees in the white house in the Omarska camp. When we reached Omarska and the white house, they forced us to sing those songs. And they trod on us also when we were being transported by buses from the Omarska camp towards the Manjaca camp. We were also forced to sing Chetnik songs. Similarly, in the buses. Once we reached Manjaca, that first night that we spent in the buses, we were also forced to sing these Chetnik songs then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn to a totally different question. You discussed this morning the arrival of helicopters. How could you recognise the helicopters, and could you identify people from these helicopters, for example, by uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could recognise those helicopters on the basis of their colour. That colour was dark green or olive-green/grey that was also used in the former JNA. Such helicopters were in the possession of the former JNA, and they had a red five-cornered star on them. The people who were in the helicopter I could not recognise because those helicopters fly over quickly, and it is impossible to recognise a face or a uniform. One can only notice human figures in the helicopter with helmets on their heads, which means that they were pilots flying the helicopters. And on their heads, they had pilots' -- I don't know what word to use. I said helmets or something to that -- like that. Which covered their heads and ears as protection. Anyway, every pilot wore something like that in a helicopter, regardless of the assignment he was on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now go in private session, because I have to mention some names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness C, do you remember the name of the commander in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the commander of the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, does it ring a bell when I mention the word "Spaga"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is familiar. It was the nickname of that man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you give us some more details about this Spaga? What did you hear from him? Was there any special relationship between him and guards? What can you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person known as Spaga, whose name I don't know, was the leader of the guards at the Manjaca camp, which means that the guards were subordinated to him. The word "Spaga" itself means something in Bosnian. But he was something quite different from what his nickname stood for. He was extremely brutal. And when we heard his name or when we learned that Spaga was coming, we all had to seek refuge in the stable. Nobody dared utter a word. If he were to enter the stable accompanied by a guard, all of us had to get up, following orders, and to stand to attention. And we stood like that for as long as he wished, until he had gone to the end of the stable and back to the door. And when he left, we were still standing, while he walked up and down. And while he was walking up and down, we didn't dare utter a word or make a sound or move. He could hit whoever he wanted to. It was up to his whim. There was nothing we could do about it. It was his personal choice. And only once he left the stable, if we got the appropriate command from the guard, then we could sit down. And this standing would last for hours. People would faint. They couldn't stand -- remain standing for so long. They were starved. So this had very bad effect upon us. People would faint. You would just hear the thud when someone fell down, but you didn't dare turn around to look and see who it was. If they were to notice you turning around, then you would get a good hiding. As for Spaga and his appearance, he was tall, quite well built. He had a powerful voice. He liked to yell and shout at us. And as I said, if somebody were to say "Spaga's coming," we would all fall silent and everybody would have to get up and wait and see what would happen. We were waiting to see what would happen. There would be frequent searches in the stable. We all had to be lined up outside the stables, and they would enter the guards and check and search everything inside where we were held. They would check all our beds where we lay and where we would spend the night. Those beds, I use that word, "bed," though it wasn't really a bed. It was just the ground, the concrete floor, and some grass and dried ferns that had dried after some time. So in fact, we were lying on the concrete, the stone, the earth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness C, this morning, you mentioned the commander of Manjaca delivering a speech -- sorry that I quote it just from the top of my head -- saying "if those who will return, they will be killed." Was this commander identical with Spaga?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This means that there was another commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the camp commander, the commander of the whole of Manjaca camp. He was superior to Spaga, to the man known as Spaga and all the others. He was the commander -- the main commander of the Manjaca camp. And I even think that he had the rank of colonel, as far as I can remember, judging by the stories among the detainees. Probably, and that is also a fact, he was an active-duty officer of the former JNA, which means he was an active-duty officer before the war in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know the name or nickname of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I have to come back to two concrete dates, because when revisiting the transcripts, there was some confusion. Could you please once again tell us the exact dates you had to spend in Omarska and you were in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be glad to repeat those dates, because this is something you can't forget easily. I arrived at the Omarska camp on the 9th of July, and I was there until the 6th of August. From the 6th of August until the 18th of December of that same year -- and that means 1992 -- I was in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. At 2.04, it's just a point in the transcript, you said that: "You don't remember the actual text of the document enabling your release."You added: "If you are interested, I can tell you why." I'm interested. Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be glad to, Your Honour. In my opinion, that paper contained wording related to us detainees printed out, written, prepared, and everything ready to be signed so that each person could individually sign that piece of paper. All those documents were the same for all the detainees. The reason why I could not remember the exact wording of that document is, number one, that we didn't have much time to read it out. All this was in great haste outside where we signed it standing up. And as soon as one signed it, one had to go out through the gate, outside the camp, where buses were ready and waiting. A very important reason for us for signing this document was that this was the only guarantee that we would be released, because without that signature we couldn't leave the Manjaca camp. There would be no freedom for us. At the time we were supposed to sign this, all we cared about was to sign it and get out. That was our aim, which ensured for us freedom and departure from that infamous camp. In brief, without a signature, you couldn't leave, there would be no freedom. And on this piece of paper, I assume it said if any one of us were to return -- or rather, that particular person who signed this document, if that person were to be arrested and caught on the ground, within the territory of the so-called Serbian Krajina, without further ado, he would be killed. And he would not have a chance of coming to the camp again. So, by summary procedure, no camp; only death. Short and sweet. And that is the reason why we had to sign it. If we wanted to leave the camp, we had no other choice. That was the only choice we had at the time. I think, and I hope, that you will understand the reason for me acting in this way, as well as for all the other detainees who signed that strange so-called document. That was unforeseeable for us. This was -- I can freely put it that way. It was blackmail by them so that we would not return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is also proof that there was ethnic cleansing. I hope that you will accept what I have said. So this was a kind of ethnic cleansing, together with the other things that happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, throughout the duration of that war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness C, can you be more specific in regard of the Chetniks. Do you have any idea about the composition of those armed and/or uniformed persons referred to by yourself as "the Chetniks"? Did they belong to the JNA, police, or security personnel, or they were paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Your Honour, as regard the term itself "the Chetniks," because a moment ago, this morning, I testified about this, I consider to be the Chetniks, the former members of the JNA, because they were the former members of the JNA after that they were no longer members of the JNA but became Chetniks. I also consider members of the police force to be Chetniks, and I also consider paramilitaries to be Chetniks regardless of how they were actually called, these paramilitary forces. Sometimes they were called after a commander who was their leader. I don't think I need to illustrate this with any example. I think that the situation is very well known, even outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I should like to focus on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So in short, I considered to be Chetniks all of them, although members of the former JNA, before the war, before the conflict in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia, were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. members of the military, members of the army which represented all ethnic groups of the former Yugoslavia. However, they betrayed the people. They attacked that very same people, or rather, peoples, who had financed them, who had armed them, this former JNA, which had been armed by the peoples of the former Yugoslavia. We all contribute -- made contributions for this former JNA, but they turned their backs to the Bosniak people and the Croatian people, and they sided with the Serb people. And they participated in the ethnic cleansing, in the killings, the persecutions, plunders, and rapes, in the creation of concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But the personnel in the camp who treated you personally, did they belong to the army, to the police, or they were paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belonged to the army, but also to the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more question: As far as I understand, nobody informed you formally and officially about the titles, positions, and names of the commanders and shift commanders of the Omarska and Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Keraterm camp is concerned, I don't know what titles they had, the guards. You probably mean what kind of ranks they had. The same goes for the Omarska camp; I'm not familiar with their ranks or titles, military ranks, titles, or what they were called. Likewise, I don't know about police ranks either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And do you know who were in command and control of the commanders and personnel of the camps? Or, in other words, who was the superiors of those commanders and shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camp commanders. The shift commanders were superior to the camp commanders [sic]. The guards were responsible to the shift commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But whom were -- the commanders and shift commanders of the camp, whom were they subordinated? Who were their superior? Do you have any idea about the names, titles, positions of those persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camp commanders were responsible to the political party, the SDS, and other municipal authorities. Also, to the police authorities up to the mayor of the municipality. The commander of the military, who were superior to the Banja Luka authorities, and the Banja Luka authorities were responsible to the Pale authorities, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the representatives, highest representatives, of those authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the names, some of them are widely known. The civilian authorities who conducted all of these operations were located in Banja Luka. As for the main body of the civilian authority, they were located at Pale and led by Karadzic. The military authorities were also there, and their leader was Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what about Prijedor municipality? What is the relationship between Banja Luka and Prijedor and the camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Prijedor, the municipality of Prijedor was in contact with the municipality of Banja Luka which had the overall control over the activities that were going on in Prijedor. Because the Prijedor authorities were subordinate to the authorities in Banja Luka. And Banja Luka was subordinate to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did you have an ID when you were detained in Omarska and Keraterm camps? Identification card, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have anything with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you been called by your name when summoned for beatings and interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was called out by my name and surname. When I was called out to go for interrogation, and also to be taken out for beatings. In any case, they had the names of all of the detainees. They had lists with names of the people who were detained in those camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. And how detainees were selected for beatings and interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say much about how they were selected. I know that they had lists of names with them, and they read out the names from those lists and called people out, which doesn't mean that they called people out in order from those lists. They would call out whoever they thought they knew by name and surname. That person would usually be the first one to be called out. And then, others were also called, but they called people out according to their wishes, at their whim, according to some kind of decision that they must have reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the last question: Did you receive any documents when you were released from the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was released from the Manjaca camp, I did not receive any personal document, because I did not have any such document in the Manjaca camp. Whatever I had was taken away from me in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness C, just to give you the possibility either to correct or to confirm what you said, at 15.18, you said: "The shift commanders were superior to the camp commanders." Did you really wanted to say this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been a grammatical error if I said "superior." It was the camp commanders who were superior to shift commanders. You know, it's easy to confuse these two words, superior and subordinate, and that probably caused the confusion and the misunderstanding. I hope Your Honours will understand. I must admit that sometimes my concentration fails me when it comes to these technical terms, superior, subordinate. So I must have confused the two words. Please accept my apologies once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question: What was the role of the Red Cross in Manjaca? And was it the International Red Cross or the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the International Red Cross at Manjaca -- and I emphasise, the International Red Cross, not the local Red Cross organisation -- was, first of all, to assist us not to starve to death, not to freeze to death. Sometimes, it snows even in September at Manjaca. So that was mainly the role of the International Red Cross, to provide us with some food, some clothes, blankets so that we would not freeze to death. However, despite their efforts, we were still hungry and cold, although at one point in time, we did start receiving this aid that I mentioned. If it wasn't for this aid, I don't know how many people would leave Manjaca alive and not leave their bones there. So the role of the International Red Cross was to try and find a way out for us, to find some solution for our situation so that we would be able to leave this infamous Manjaca camp. For us, it was a very slow and lengthy process. We didn't know what would happen. But in the end, we were told the good news, that is, that we would be taken elsewhere. However, all this information was not reliable. " [In English] And down about 15 lines, Mr. President, is a sentence that begins in the middle of the paragraph: [Interpretation] "It is true that the fault is not only on the part of the guys who held this barricade, but also their leaders who will be stripped of their ranks." [In English] And then just one sentence below the box about 12 lines: [Interpretation] "We offered them to stay at the front and to be transferred to the rear, if in that way they were to save face and avoid military court martial, but they rejected this."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have major objections, only we don't see the relevance. Whatever you decide, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional clarification. But it remains a problem that we still have some additional remarks in handwriting. And probably, it should be revisited by the translation unit to that extent.

utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the article that is only on the lower half of the page. For some reason here -- I think, for reasons of clarity of the small print, we went from one page to 2, but only this article which is on the second page, left side, is, I think, of interest --

utterances.text: Dr. Donia.

utterances.text: "How to survive, that's the question."

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: In these limitations admitted into evidence SK40B. 41?

utterances.text: We do have an objection to this document. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Your comments, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as to the date, if you go to the original version, which is in Cyrillic, but the date is very clear in the first paragraph of the document, that it is in fact 17.01, 92, 17 January 1992. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence SK41A, SK41B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not admitted into evidence.

utterances.text: The next exhibit would be SK44, which is the transcript of Dr. Donia's evidence in the... Mr. President, it's hard work, whatever I say. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection as earlier, Your Honour.

Again, leading us -- not to be overly suspicious, but at least leading us to indicate that we might have an extremely grave problem with authenticity on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as SK45A and 45B. utterances.text: These, Mr. President - in fact 46 and 47 - are part of the SDS minutes that we dealt with under Exhibit 12. So I assume that Mr. Ostojic will probably be making the same objection that he did in respect of Exhibit 12.

utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously with respect to Exhibit Number 46, we did ask questions of the witness, particularly the items that were referenced to Dr. Stakic. utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.text: We may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to this exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please comment on the relevance, Dr. Donia.

utterances.text: Yes, this article, on the second page of the upper left-hand corner, reports an event that I referred to in my testimony of the appointment of various members of government in the Serbian assembly or municipality of Prijedor on, I think it was, the 16th of April, 1991 -- I'm sorry, 1992.

utterances.text: So it's only this article in -- on the top of the left-hand side, an article signed by R. Mutic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Under our guidelines, admitted into evidence but only on the second page, the top article, from Mutic, from the newspaper "Glas" of 18 of August, 1992 -- April.

utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I realise that we've gone well over time, but if I could just revisit one issue with you, and I know Mr. Koumjian may want to make some representations on this as well. I would only I think emphasise the reason why you received abbreviated evidence in this trial was because of the pressure on the Office of the Prosecutor to shorten witness testimony. That is why it was produced as an annex, but I would emphasise, an annex to a principle report, the report of Brdjanin/Talic. It is in that sense a composite part of that main report. And by amputating the main part of the report, it is in very much, in many respects, it's incomplete. You don't have all of the evidence before you. So I would emphasise to you, I realise you have made a decision on this, that for you to have a full picture, a comprehensive picture, on events outside of Prijedor are relevant to this case, you should in my respectful submission either admit the transcripts of that hearing from the Brdjanin/Talic case or the report of which the annex is a part. And I think Mr. Koumjian just spoke to me very briefly about a specific example of evidence that was led in this case. I wasn't present when that evidence was led, which I think will probably reflect the point that masses of evidence are coming out in the courtroom through other witnesses that were referred to in Dr. Donia's report in Brdjanin/Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that we don't want to revisit questions and decisions we once made. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.text: Now, we have an entire binder, the Donia exhibits SK1 until -- correct SK50 or 51? SK51. utterances.text: The next witness is Witness 31. And that will be the only witness we have available this week. The witness will take I believe more than a day, but I'm not sure how long that witness will be.

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Then you had -- it was convincing that a time limit of seven days would be arrived today. Please take the floor for this purpose.

utterances.text: Yes. About a week ago last Thursday, Your Honour, I believe made an oral order on the identification parade or lineup of a witness. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I am confused. Rule 73 has changed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Limiting the interlocutory appeals to questions of jurisdiction only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it's time enough for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Because the way I read the rule, the old rule, we must get the certification within seven days. Is that correct, or not? utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: We can respond briefly now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to take care of the interpreters, and it's no longer possible. It is a matter of a minute? No, before we start. It's an important issue, and it's no longer possible to go on. utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think actually tomorrow would be the seven days if we count, so I can hold off on filing until we discuss this tomorrow morning. I will prepare the motion tonight and then we can hold off on filing until we discuss this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should start tomorrow with the witness. The witness shouldn't wait. And, in addition, as we had already 35 minutes overtime -- we shouldn't start tomorrow earlier than 9.30. We stay adjourned and resume tomorrow 9.30.
